title: Will Vodery's lessons on scoring and accompanying singers
summary: A veteran arranger told the band to stay under the singer and to score in ink, checking every four bars; he reportedly had Gershwin as copyist.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I don't remember... I was so busy trying to stay in that band, that I never remember when anybody got fired, what the reason was getting fired for. But that was a band. It was a fabulous band, a great band. Will Roziere(?) was our...
...me... Because for some reason he got a liking to me.

He was the greatest thing that happened to me. Because he told me so much about music. Because he was the one who told me that... He told the band. He said, "Listen. The band is accompanying the singer." So that means you're supposed to be under the singer. He said, "You ain't never supposed to be louder than a singer." And he wrote music... We had never played that kind of music before.

Scored in ink. And he told us that. And he taught me about scoring. He said, 'When you score, score four bars and then check it.' Check every note to see it's right. You see, this is how you keep from making mistakes. And he told me he used to give his copyists a dollar for every mistake he made, otherwise he would tell his copyists to copy everything they saw on the score -- don't be changing nothin' he wrote on the score. And he was right. I'd never seen nobody score in ink.
He told me one time George Gershwin was his copyist, when he was doing the Ziegfield shows.
And that stuff sounded so good, man.
